characteristics.harvestSeason: Spring, harvested 7–10 days earlier than Tie Guan Yin

description.short: One of the most aromatic Anxi oolongs, boasting an intense floral fragrance reminiscent of sweet osmanthus
description.overview: Regarded as the 'sister' of Tie Guan Yin: hailing from the same county with similar light oxidation, but crafted from a distinct cultivar that yields a notably more intense, almost perfumed floral profile.
description.leaf: Tightly rolled light-green pearls, slightly brighter and yellower than Tie Guan Yin
description.aroma: Intensely floral, reminiscent of sweet osmanthus and blooming magnolia, with delicate fruity undertones
description.taste: Vibrant, floral, and naturally sweet, with a lighter body compared to Tie Guan Yin
description.processing: Plucking → withering → gentle tossing/shaking for minimal edge oxidation → fixation (kill-green) → ball-rolling → light drying without roasting

history.origin: The name translates to 'Golden Osmanthus' due to its golden infusion and dazzling floral fragrance resembling blossoming osmanthus flowers.
history.development: Bred from the Huang Dan ('Yellow Dan' or 'Yellow Bud') cultivar in Anxi County, it is prized primarily for its exceptionally early budding and aromatic intensity rather than body heaviness.
history.modern: Due to its very early harvest window (earlier than most other Anxi oolongs), it traditionally heralds the opening of the spring tea season.
interestingFacts: Celebrated among local tea farmers with the saying: 'Golden liquor, fragrance carrying ten li'—highlighting its penetrating bouquet.
Despite its dazzling aroma, the body is relatively light and delicate compared to Tie Guan Yin, creating a fascinating contrast between scent and palate.
